column1: Capacity, scheduling, the shared spine, and coordination, grouped into rollup categories. The analytics columns (H-R) are collapsed by default - expand them for the scoring detail. Every column is defined in the Column key just below.

column3: Stable code for the variable (SH- shared, C- capacity, S- scheduling, CO- coordination). Links to the full definition on Tab 1; never renumbered.
Which part of the model the variable belongs to: Shared (used by both), Capacity (supply), Scheduling (allocation), or Coordination (execution). Color-banded down the sheet.
The capacity, scheduling, or coordination factor. Plain name here; the full definition and example live on Tab 1.

How firm the rule is. Hard = the visit fails if it isn't honored. Soft = optimize toward it, bend under pressure. Structural = a fixed fact of supply or geography. Event = a demand trigger. Derived = a computed value. Config = a policy-set constant.
Is this a day-one must-have for the software? Yes / Maybe / No. Sets the scoring Weight.
How far software should go on the variable. Control = it can decide and act. Assist = it proposes and a person confirms. Read = it only surfaces information and a person decides.
Plain-English reason for the posture, and what to watch on that row.
Who the variable comes from: Clinician, Patient, Caregiver, Branch, Geography, or System. Lets you filter by whose world it lives in.

How it is handled today. In-system = already in a system of record. Manual = done by hand. Tacit = lives in someone's head, not written down. Not captured = nowhere yet. Tacit or Not-captured on a must-have is where the biggest opportunity sits.
The system(s) the data comes from today: HCHB, Workday, Routing, Census, Manual, Config, Telephony, or Derived.
Quantitative (countable, measurable) or Qualitative (judgment-based). Flags where a vendor rating will be subjective.
How safely software can act on the variable - High / Medium / Low. The input behind the Automation Posture.
Optional deeper view, hidden by default. Internal reference notes on why a variable is safe or unsafe to automate.
Category or Variable. Category rows are the group headers; Variable rows are the scored items. Lets Tab 3 total the variables without counting the headers.
Short code tying each variable to its category header (e.g. CAP-A), so Tab 3 can total a whole category cleanly.
Scoring weight from MVP Req.: Yes 3 / Maybe 1 / No 0. Turns the checklist into a priority ranking - a missing must-have costs the score more than a missing nice-to-have. Live formula.
A knockout flag (Y/N). Y when the variable is a Hard or Structural must-have - a product that cannot do it should be disqualified no matter how well it scores elsewhere. Live formula.

Y where a vendor's built-in way of working could contradict how Compassus already operates, so the product would fight the branch instead of fitting it. Example: the tool models service area by ZIP when Compassus manages territory by drive-time - adopting it would force a change to an established rule. These are the rows to probe hardest in a demo, and the reason the scorecard tracks not just what a product COVERS and where it leaves GAPS, but where it CONFLICTS.

Which of the three target modules the variable is built or bought into - Capacity Management, Scheduling Engine, or Patient Engagement. An additional grouping over the inventory, not a replacement for Layer or Rollup Key; every join still joins on ID. Added 2026-08-19 from the target-architecture handoff.
